sentence: Tramadol belongs to a group of medicines called opioids.
note: Search summary of NHS/NHS-trust pages: tramadol is from a group of medicines called opioids.

sentence: It is used to relieve moderately severe pain.
note: Used to relieve moderately severe pain.

sentence: That can include pain after surgery and pain from long-term conditions such as joint pain.
note: May be used for pain caused by surgery and chronic conditions such as joint pain (blended summary; attributed to NHS About page with trust pages).

sentence: The NHS says standard tramadol starts to ease pain after about half an hour to an hour, and the relief wears off after some hours.
note: NHS common questions: less pain around 30 to 60 minutes after standard tramadol; relief wears off after 4 to 6 hours.

sentence: Tramadol raises serotonin levels in the brain as well as acting like other opioids, which is why it can interact with some other medicines.
note: Royal Devon NHS leaflet: tramadol increases serotonin levels in the brain, raising the risk of serotonin toxicity with certain other medicines; pharmacology summary notes serotonin and noradrenaline effects.

sentence: Taking too much may cause strong sleepiness, sickness or dizziness, difficulty breathing, or loss of consciousness, and this needs emergency treatment in hospital.
note: NHS how and when to take: too much may cause very sleepy, sick, dizzy, difficult to breathe, unconscious, emergency hospital treatment.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for serious reactions, and not to drive there alone.
note: NHS side effects page: emergency list; ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance rather than driving yourself to A&E.

sentence: Common side effects include feeling sleepy, tired, dizzy or spaced out, and feeling or being sick.
note: NHS side effects: common effects sleepy, tired, dizzy, spaced out, feeling/being sick.

sentence: The NHS says serious side effects affect fewer than 1 in 100 people.
note: Serious side effects happen in less than 1 in 100 people.

sentence: The NHS lists a seizure (fit), and difficulty breathing or short, shallow breathing, as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.
note: NHS side effects emergency section: seizure; breathing difficulties or short shallow breathing; call 999 / ask for ambulance.

sentence: A serious allergic reaction is rare, with signs such as swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or trouble breathing, and the NHS says to call 999.
note: NHS: rare serious allergic reaction; swelling of lips, mouth, throat or tongue, trouble breathing; call 999.

sentence: A hospital leaflet describes serotonin syndrome, with agitation, confusion, fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, dilated pupils and muscle twitching, and advises urgent medical help.
note: Royal Devon leaflet lists these serotonin toxicity symptoms and advises seeking urgent medical help; the 999 wording for this was not retrieved.

sentence: For concerns that are not emergencies, the NHS points people to a doctor or NHS 111.
note: NHS side effects page: non-emergency concerns, call doctor or 111.

sentence: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to tramadol.
note: NHS common questions: it's possible to become addicted.

sentence: Signs include finding it hard to stop or feeling a need to take it more often than necessary.
note: As the NHS page: difficult to stop, or need to take it more often than necessary.

sentence: Stopping can cause withdrawal symptoms, which the NHS lists as agitation, anxiety, panic attacks, palpitations, trouble sleeping, shaking, sweating, body aches and restlessness.
note: NHS common questions list of withdrawal symptoms.

sentence: The same leaflet also mentions stomach cramps, diarrhoea, a runny nose and low mood, and advises against stopping suddenly.
note: Royal Devon leaflet lists these and advises against stopping suddenly.

sentence: The NHS advises talking to a doctor about stopping or about worries over addiction, and long-term users may have a plan for how and when to stop.
note: NHS: talk to your doctor if you want to stop or worry about addiction; long-term users may have a treatment plan.

sentence: The NHS says monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), which treat depression or Parkinson's disease, should not be taken with tramadol.
note: NHS other-medicines page: do not take MAOIs, examples moclobemide, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline.

sentence: An NHS trust guideline says SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, triptans and St John's wort can add to serotonin-related side effects and may lead to serotonin syndrome.
note: Hertfordshire NHS trust guideline (older document): SSRIs, TCAs, St John's wort, 5HT1 agonists such as sumatriptan raise serotonin side effects.

sentence: Some medicines can weaken its effect, including carbamazepine, buprenorphine, ondansetron and rifampicin, and the NHS notes its list is not complete.
note: NHS page names these and says the list is not complete; check the leaflet.

sentence: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with tramadol because side effects such as sleepiness are more likely.
note: NHS: best not to drink alcohol; more likely to get side effects like feeling sleepy.

sentence: On driving, the NHS says not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery if tramadol makes a person sleepy, dizzy or clumsy.
note: NHS advice: do not drive a car, ride a bike or use tools/machinery if it makes you sleepy, dizzy or clumsy (blended summary, NHS tramadol pages).

sentence: The NHS says tramadol is not known to cause problems with a baby's development, but more studies are needed to confirm this.
note: NHS pregnancy page.

sentence: Taken near the end of pregnancy, it can cause withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, such as feeding problems or needing help with breathing.
note: NHS pregnancy page.

sentence: If the baby is healthy, the NHS says tramadol may be possible during breastfeeding.
note: NHS: if your baby is healthy you may be able to take it while breastfeeding.

sentence: The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service advises the lowest effective amount for the shortest time, says babies under 2 months are at most risk, and advises watching for drowsiness in the baby.
note: SPS article: lowest effective dose for shortest duration; neonates and infants under 2 months at most risk; watch for sleepiness.

sentence: Guidance says tramadol is avoided or used with great caution in people with epilepsy or a history of addiction.
note: Hertfordshire trust guideline: great caution with history of addiction/dependence; avoid with epilepsy or seizure susceptibility. Sussex bulletin less absolute (not cited).
